newsitem.title: USA: Intel price cuts to fuel lower PC prices.
newsitem.headline: Intel price cuts to fuel lower PC prices.

text.p: Intel Corp's plans for its quarterly price cuts on Pentium processors are expected to lead to slightly lower prices for personal computers, but analysts do not expect a PC price war as a result.
On Thursday, Intel said it plans its usual price cuts at the end of the month, but a spokesman declined to say by how much prices will be cut on its widely-used Pentium chip.

Some analysts speculated that in expectation of rival chips, such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc's new K6, Intel will cut Pentium prices more than usual, from 25 to 30 percent. Intel's shares fell as a result, losing 4-1/4 to 133.
"This continues to fuel normal PC demand," said Kimball Brown, an analyst with Dataquest Inc in San Jose, Calif. "This is the normal stuff that keeps stimulating the market."
Consumers will benefit, as PC makers will be able to offer "more bang for the buck," as in PCs with faster processing speeds at lower prices.

"The Intel price cuts should be positive to PC vendors," said Daniel Ries, a Nomura Research analyst. "It lowers their cost of building the system. Some of the money they save will be passed on to consumers and they can offer a more powerful system at a cheaper price."

Analysts said that direct sellers of PCs, such as Gateway 2000 Inc and Dell Computer Corp, would be the first PC makers to cut prices, because they have the smallest amounts of inventory on hand and build their PCs to order. "The direct guys will be able to move the price cuts through faster because they are not carrying any inventory, and everyone will follow," said Louis Mazzucchelli, an analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison. "We will have lower PC prices for a while...End users will benefit."
"Yes, we typically pass on those savings to the customer," said a Dell spokesman, of Intel's anticipated price cuts.

"Our business model and our build-to-order manufacturing process give us a distinct advantage to do so before most of our competitors," the Dell spokesman added. He declined to comment on Intel's expected actions or on how much Dell might cut prices in the future.
The most recent industry-wide price cuts took place in early February, when the majority of PC makers cut prices on Pentium and Pentium Pro-based PCs, servers and notebooks.
Some analysts said average PC prices may dip slightly from around $2,500, or consumers will get more, such as faster processors, more disk space or more memory, for the same price.

But analysts do not expect any drastic pricing moves, such as the PC price wars that started in the June of 1992, when Compaq Computer Corp unfurled new-lower priced PCs which led to huge price cuts in the industry and a new model for lower profit margins.

"I don't think it will lead to a price war," said Daniel Kunstler, a JP Morgan analyst. "I would expect some discipline...if they were to engage in a price war, it would take down earnings estimates. My expectation is that there will be some lowering of prices, but in a disciplined fashion."
Later this year, prices will likely drop again, after the Pentium II is launched and before autumn new product launches.
